insider_note: 1/(1+x) is exactly the derivative of log(1+x) — the same f(x)·f′(x) shape as sinx·cosx, just written with a logarithm instead of a trig function.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Substitute t = log(1 + x)
steps.why: d/dx[log(1+x)] = 1/(1+x), so the whole factor dx/(1+x) converts to dt in one step, leaving just the outer factor log(1+x) = t to integrate as a plain power of t.
common_mistakes: Trying integration by parts on log(1+x)/(1+x), which is unnecessary once the substitution is spotted.
Substituting t=1+x instead of t=log(1+x), which does not remove the log from the integrand.
steps.memory_tip: The integrand IS f(x)·f′(x) for f(x)=log(1+x) — the same shape as ∫sinx cosx dx, solved by t=f(x).

steps.label: Integrate and back-substitute for the final answer
steps.why: ∫t dt = t²/2 + c is the plain power rule, and substituting t=log(1+x) back in gives the final answer as a square of the logarithm.
common_mistakes: Writing log[(1+x)²]/2 instead of [log(1+x)]²/2 — the SQUARE belongs to the whole log, not inside it.
Forgetting to substitute log(1+x) back in for t.
steps.memory_tip: The square applies to the WHOLE log(1+x), not to what is inside the log — [log(1+x)]², never log[(1+x)²].
